nameStory: This tiny water flea doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Picripleuroxus denticulatus. The genus name Picripleuroxus comes from Greek words meaning "bitter side hook," likely referring to the small spines along its shell, while "denticulatus" means "with small teeth" - describing the tiny tooth-like projections on its carapace.
description: Picripleuroxus denticulatus is a microscopic water flea, one of the many tiny crustaceans that drift through New England's freshwater ponds and lakes. This translucent creature measures less than half a millimeter long - smaller than a grain of sand - and lives inside a clear, clam-like shell called a carapace. Like other water fleas, it swims with jerky, hopping motions using its large, branched antennae as oars. You'll need a microscope or strong magnifying glass to see the intricate details that make this species special.

idTips.label: Shell teeth
idTips.description: The rear edge of the transparent shell has distinctive small, tooth-like projections that feel sharp if you could touch them - these are the "denticles" that give this species its name

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Extremely small, roughly oval shell that's compressed from side to side, measuring about 0.3-0.4mm long - imagine a tiny transparent clam

idTips.label: Shell sculpture
idTips.description: The shell surface appears faintly textured under magnification, with subtle lines and patterns etched into the transparent carapace

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Large, branched swimming antennae that extend well beyond the shell opening, creating the characteristic jerky swimming motion

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Nearly colorless and transparent, though the internal organs may appear as darker spots within the clear shell

habitat: Found in the shallow, weedy areas of New England's freshwater ponds and lakes, particularly where aquatic plants provide plenty of organic matter to filter-feed on. This species prefers areas with soft sediments and abundant microscopic algae and bacteria. Look for them in the littoral zone - the near-shore area where sunlight penetrates to support plant growth.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin building as water temperatures warm, though you'd need to collect water samples and examine them microscopically to observe these tiny creatures.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when algae and bacteria are most plentiful, making this the best time to find specimens in pond samples.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may remain steady into early fall, but cooler temperatures begin to slow reproduction and activity levels.
seasonality.winter: Populations crash in winter, surviving primarily as dormant eggs that can withstand freezing temperatures until spring thaw.

funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, this tiny water flea can live for several weeks and produce dozens of offspring without ever mating - females simply clone themselves until environmental stress triggers the need for sexual reproduction and those hardy winter eggs.
confusionNotes: This species is easily confused with other members of the Chydoridae family, but the small teeth along the rear shell margin are distinctive - think of them as nature's microscopic saw blade that sets this species apart from its smooth-shelled relatives.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name might seem intimidating, but it's actually quite descriptive once you break it down - scientists often use these detailed Latin names for microscopic species because common names simply don't exist for most of the tiny creatures that make up freshwater ecosystems.
compareHints: Since this is the only Picripleuroxus species recorded in New England, compare it with other chydorid water fleas like Chydorus species. Unlike the more rounded Chydorus, Picripleuroxus has a more elongated shell shape and those diagnostic small teeth on the rear margin. The shell sculpture and denticles are key features that separate it from other tiny freshwater crustaceans in the same family.
